It is a common misconception that "same core count and clock speed" equals the "exact same CPU." While the A19 and A19 Pro both feature a 6-core setup (2 performance, 4 efficiency) running at 4.26 GHz, Apple has essentially built the A19 Pro with a "larger brain" and better plumbing.

Here is why they aren't technically the same under the hood:

1. The Cache Moat

Think of cache as the CPU’s ultra-fast "short-term memory." The A19 Pro has significantly more of it:

  • L2 Cache (Performance Cores): 16MB on the Pro vs. 8MB on the base A19.
  • System-Level Cache (SLC): 32MB on the Pro vs. 12MB on the base A19.
  • Efficiency Cores: The Pro also gets a 50% increase in last-level cache for its efficiency cores.

This extra cache is why, in real-world benchmarks, the A19 Pro consistently scores 6–8% higher in single-core tasks than the base A19, even though they are running at the exact same clock speed. The Pro chip spends less time waiting for data to travel from the RAM.

2. Front-End Architecture

The A19 Pro includes architectural improvements that aren't in the base A19:

  • Branch Prediction: The Pro has more advanced logic for predicting what code will run next, reducing "stalls" in processing.
  • Front-End Bandwidth: The "pipe" that feeds instructions into the CPU cores is wider on the Pro.

3. Thermal Sustenance

Since you're looking at a high-end MacBook Pro soon, you’re likely familiar with how heat kills performance. On the iPhone 17 side, the Pro and Pro Max use a vapor chamber cooling system (the first in an iPhone).

  • The base A19 is limited by standard graphite sheets.
  • Under a heavy load (like a 20-minute gaming session), the A19 Pro can maintain its peak 4.26 GHz speed for much longer, while the base A19 has to "throttle" down to prevent overheating.

title: Prompted Does sensor size or aperture effect depth of field

safeHtmlItem.html:
Both sensor size and aperture have a significant impact on depth of field (DoF), though they influence the image in different ways.

Aperture

Aperture is the most direct way to control depth of field. It refers to the opening in the lens that allows light to reach the sensor.

  • Large Aperture (Small f-number, e.g., f/1.8): Creates a shallow depth of field. This results in a sharp subject with a blurred background (bokeh).
  • Small Aperture (Large f-number, e.g., f/16): Creates a deep depth of field. This keeps more of the scene, from the foreground to the background, in focus.

Sensor Size

The relationship between sensor size and depth of field is slightly more indirect because it usually involves changes in focal length or distance to maintain the same framing.

  • Larger Sensors (Full Frame): Generally produce a shallower depth of field for a given field of view. To get the same "shot" as a smaller sensor, you either have to move closer to the subject or use a longer focal length, both of which decrease DoF.
  • Smaller Sensors (Crop/APS-C/Micro 4/3): Generally produce a deeper depth of field. Because of the "crop factor," you typically use wider lenses or stand further back to frame the subject, which increases the area in focus.

Summary Table

FeatureChangeEffect on Depth of Field
ApertureWider (Lower f-stop)Shallower (More blur)
ApertureNarrower (Higher f-stop)Deeper (More in focus)
Sensor SizeLarger (Full Frame)Shallower (at equivalent framing)
Sensor SizeSmaller (Crop)Deeper (at equivalent framing)

title: Prompted Why is it called breaking bad

The title "Breaking Bad" is rooted in a regional colloquialism from the American South, specifically Virginia and the Carolinas.

Meaning and Origin

  • The Definition: To "break bad" means to deviate from a legal or moral path. It describes a person who has suddenly turned toward a life of crime, violence, or general "hell-raising."
  • Vince Gilligan’s Usage: Series creator Vince Gilligan, who grew up in Virginia, used the phrase to describe the fundamental premise of the show: a straight-laced, law-abiding citizen (Walter White) making a conscious decision to go rogue.
  • The Transformation: In the pilot episode, Jesse Pinkman actually uses the phrase when questioning Walt’s motivations, asking why a "straight" person like him would suddenly decide to "break bad."

Symbolism in the Show

The title serves as a literal roadmap for Walter White's character arc. While many TV protagonists remain relatively static, Gilligan famously pitched the show as the story of "taking Mr. Chips and turning him into Scarface." The phrase captures that specific, irreversible pivot from a "good" life to a "bad" one.

title: Prompted Strength train before or after run

The ideal timing for strength training depends on whether your priority is building running endurance or maximal strength. For most runners rebuilding their base, the "Running First" approach is usually best.

The General Rule: Run First

If your goal is to rebuild endurance and speed, you should perform your run before your strength training.

  • Fresh Mechanics: Running while fatigued from a leg workout can lead to poor form, which increases the risk of aggravating your shin pain.
  • Energy Specificity: You want your muscle glycogen and nervous system to be fresh for your 6 mph intervals.
  • The Window: Ideally, wait at least 6 to 24 hours between a hard run and a strength session. If you must do them in the same block, run first, take a short break (and a snack), then lift.

When to Strength Train First

There is one specific scenario where you might flip the order:

  • Injury Prevention Priority: If your shins or glutes are so weak that your running form "collapses" immediately, doing a very light "activation" set (not a full workout) before a run can "wake up" the muscles.
  • Hypertrophy: If your primary goal was gaining muscle mass rather than running performance, you would lift first. However, for your current goals, this is likely counterproductive.

Optimal Weekly Structure

Since you are training 1–2 times per week for strength, here is how to slot it in:

DayActivityTiming Note
Option A (The "Hard Day" Method)Run AM / Strength PMKeeps your "hard" days hard and your "easy" days for total recovery.
Option B (The "Split Day" Method)Run Tuesday / Strength WednesdayBest for recovery if you find your legs are too shaky to lift after a run.

How to Manage the "Heavy Leg" Feeling

When you start 1–2 sessions a week, your first few runs after lifting will feel "heavy" or sluggish. This is normal and usually dissipates after 2–3 weeks as your body adapts to the new stimulus. Do not let the heavy feeling discourage you; it is a sign of your muscles adapting to handle more load.

  • Cancer Alley & Sharon Lavine: The video highlights St. James Parish, Louisiana, where Sharon Lavine fought to stop a $9.4 billion plastics plant in a predominantly Black community [07:12]. Her grassroots activism earned her the Goldman Environmental Prize and has delayed the plant for years [08:12].

The "Success" of Cleanups and PFAS

The narrator visits the Indian Bend Wash in Scottsdale, Arizona, once considered a model for EPA success [09:49]. However, he notes that while old chemicals (TCE/PCE) were removed, the site is now being re-investigated for PFAS ("forever chemicals") [10:30]. These chemicals were not monitored in the 1980s and represent a new, widespread challenge for modern cleanups [12:04].

Current Status of the Law

  • Funding: The "polluter pays" tax expired in 1995, shifting cleanup costs to taxpayers for 26 years [13:54]. In 2021, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act reinstated this tax [14:26].
  • New Designations: In 2024, the EPA officially designated the two most common PFAS chemicals as hazardous substances, giving the agency legal authority to force polluters to clean them up [14:33].

The video concludes by urging viewers to research their local area using the EPA's website to stay aware and informed [15:20].

title: Prompted What can I do at home instead for strength training

safeHtmlItem.html:
Since you are working out at home, the focus shifts to using gravity and tempo to create the resistance needed for running gains. You can still build significant strength for your 3-mile runs and interval sessions without a rack of dumbbells.

Home Strength Routine for Runners

No equipment needed, but a chair or sturdy elevated surface is helpful.

ExerciseReps/TimeFocus AreaWhy for Runners?
Bulgarian Split Squats3 Sets of 10 (each leg)Quads/GlutesBest "bang for buck" for single-leg power.

Calf Raises (Slow)3 Sets of 15–20Lower Leg/ShinsCrucial for your shin pain. 3s up, 3s down.
Single-Leg Glute Bridges3 Sets of 12 (each leg)Posterior ChainPrevents the "hips dropping" late in a run.
Copenhagen Planks3 Sets of 30s (each side)Inner Thigh/CoreHigh-level stability for lateral hip strength.

Making Bodyweight "Heavy"

Since you don't have weights to add, use these three variables to ensure you are actually building strength rather than just doing cardio:

  1. Tempo (Time Under Tension): Don't rush. Take 3 full seconds to lower yourself into a squat or lunge. This builds tendon strength, which is vital for your shin health.
  2. Isometrics: Hold the bottom of a split squat for 2–3 seconds before pushing back up. This forces more muscle fiber recruitment.
  3. Unilateral Focus: Always prioritize single-leg movements. Since running is essentially 1,000+ single-leg hops per mile, bilateral squats (two legs) are less effective for your specific goals.

Timing for Your Schedule

Since you are rebuilding, try to do this routine on your "off" days or at least 6 hours after a run. Doing strength work immediately before a run can compromise your form and potentially aggravate those shins.

Noticeable Milestone

By week 4 of doing this twice weekly, you should notice that your "off" pace (the 4 mph walking/jogging intervals) feels much more stable and that your ankles feel "snappier" when you transition back to 6 mph.

  • 12+ Weeks (Injury Resilience): This is the long-term payoff. By this point, the structural changes in your tendons and muscles significantly reduce the flare-ups of shin pain or general aches that often derail a training block.

title: Prompted What about strength training 1-2 times per week

safeHtmlItem.html:
Strength training 1–2 times per week is often the "missing link" for runners rebuilding endurance and speed. While core work stabilizes your chassis, full-body strength training upgrades the engine and the suspension.

Key Benefits for Runners

  • Improved Running Economy: Lifting heavy or explosive weights improves how efficiently your muscles use oxygen. Research consistently shows that runners who strength train can maintain a faster pace at the same level of cardiovascular effort.
  • Injury Resilience: Strengthening the connective tissues (tendons and ligaments) and correcting muscle imbalances (like weak glutes or hamstrings) significantly reduces the risk of common overuse injuries like runner’s knee or IT band syndrome.
  • Increased Power Output: For speed development, strength training improves "neuromuscular coordination"—essentially teaching your brain to recruit more muscle fibers simultaneously for a more powerful "push-off" with every stride.
  • Delayed Fatigue: A stronger muscle takes longer to reach its failure point. In the context of building back endurance, this means your legs won't feel "dead" as early in your long runs.

Is 1–2 Times Per Week Enough?

Yes. For a runner, the goal is supplementary strength, not hypertrophy (bodybuilding).

  • Maintenance vs. Gain: One session per week is typically enough to maintain existing strength, while two sessions per week is the "sweet spot" for making noticeable gains in power and injury prevention without overtaxing your recovery for running workouts.
  • The "Heavy" Factor: To see the most benefit for speed, focus on lower repetitions (5–8) with heavier weights or explosive bodyweight movements (plyometrics) rather than high-repetition "toning" exercises.

Most Effective Exercises for Runners

  • Compound Lower Body: Weighted Squats, Deadlifts, or Lunges.
  • Single-Leg Stability: Bulgarian Split Squats or Single-Leg Deadlifts (crucial since running is a series of single-leg hops).
  • Posterior Chain: Calf Raises and Hamstring Curls to protect the lower legs.
  • Upper Body: Rows or Overhead Presses to assist with arm drive and posture.

title: Prompted  How much of an effect on running training to build back up endurance and some speed would a core workout of about 20 minutes 1-2 times per week have? Is it a noticeable difference?

safeHtmlItem.html:
Adding a 20-minute core session 1–2 times per week won't replace aerobic mileage, but it serves as a critical "force multiplier" for your running economy and injury prevention. While it might not directly increase your $VO_2$ max, it allows you to utilize your existing cardiovascular fitness more efficiently.

Primary Effects on Performance

  • Posture Maintenance: As you fatigue during endurance runs, your pelvis tends to tilt and your torso slumps. A stronger core keeps your hips stabilized and your spine upright, preventing the "leaking" of energy that occurs when your body sways or collapses.
  • Power Transfer: Your core acts as the bridge between your upper and lower body. A stable midsection ensures that the force generated by your arms and legs is directed into forward momentum rather than being absorbed by a shaky torso.
  • Late-Race Speed: When building back speed, core strength helps you maintain a high cadence and proper knee drive even when your legs feel heavy during the final intervals of a workout.

Is the Difference Noticeable?

You likely won't feel a "boost" during the first mile, but the difference becomes apparent in two specific scenarios:

  1. The Final 25% of Long Runs: You will notice less lower-back aching and a decreased urge to "shuffle" your feet.
  2. Uphill Grinds: A stable core allows for better hip flexion, making inclines feel less taxing on your primary movers (quads and glutes).

Recommended Focus Areas

For a runner, "core" should mean more than just sit-ups. To see a noticeable difference, prioritize these movements:

  • Anti-Rotation: Movements like the Plank with Shoulder Taps or Dead Bugs to resist unwanted torso twisting.
  • Posterior Chain: Glute Bridges or Supermans to support the lower back and power the stride.
  • Lateral Stability: Side Planks to strengthen the obliques and medius, which prevent the hips from dropping during the single-leg stance phase of running.

title: Prompted average travel expense reimbursement when using your car for a company trip

safeHtmlItem.html:
For 2026, the average travel expense reimbursement is typically based on the IRS standard mileage rate. Most companies use this rate as it is the federal benchmark for the cost of operating a vehicle.

Current 2026 Mileage Rates

As of January 1, 2026, the IRS has set the following rates for the use of a car, van, pickup, or panel truck:

  • Business Use: 72.5 cents per mile (up 2.5 cents from 2025).
  • Medical/Moving: 20.5 cents per mile (for qualified active-duty military and intelligence community members).
  • Charitable Service: 14 cents per mile (unchanged, as this is set by statute).

Key Considerations for Reimbursement

  • Company Discretion: While 72.5 cents is the standard, employers are not legally required to use this exact rate. However, if they pay more than the IRS rate, the excess is generally considered taxable income for the employee.
  • What It Covers: The standard rate is designed to cover all costs associated with the vehicle, including gas, oil, repairs, tires, insurance, and depreciation.
  • Actual Expenses: Alternatively, you can calculate the actual cost of operating your vehicle (gas, maintenance, etc.), though this requires much more detailed record-keeping and is less common for standard company reimbursements.
  • Commuting Exclusion: Standard mileage rates typically do not apply to your normal commute from home to your regular place of work; they only apply to travel between job sites, to client meetings, or for other business-related errands.

title: Prompted does supercell host thier own servers or is it cloud based? say brawl stars has a doublign in popularity in a week, how do the servers handle that>

safeHtmlItem.html:
Supercell uses a cloud-based infrastructure, primarily through Amazon Web Services (AWS). While they don't own the physical data centers, they manage thousands of virtual servers that power games like Brawl Stars and Clash of Clans.

To handle a sudden doubling in popularity (a "spike") in a single week, they rely on a combination of automated systems and pre-planned capacity.

How Supercell Uses the Cloud

Supercell doesn't just use one big server; they use a distributed network to keep latency low.

  • AWS Regions & Local Zones: They host "battle servers" in multiple locations globally. When you play Brawl Stars, you are typically connected to an AWS Local Zone—a mini data center located in a major city—to ensure your ping stays below 80ms.
  • Database Management: They use Amazon Aurora for their player data (like your trophies and skins). It’s designed to be "high-availability," meaning it can handle massive traffic without the game crashing.

Handling a 100% Increase in Players

If Brawl Stars doubled its player count in a week, the system would handle it through several key mechanisms:

1. Auto-Scaling Groups

Supercell uses Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling. The system monitors metrics like CPU usage and active connections. If the existing servers are 70% full, the cloud automatically "spins up" hundreds of new server instances in minutes. Once the crowd leaves, it "spins them down" to save money.

2. AWS Countdown & Capacity Reservations

For massive events (like a global launch or a huge update), Supercell uses a service called AWS Countdown. This is essentially a "reservation" system where they tell Amazon, "We expect 2 million concurrent players on Tuesday." Amazon ensures that the physical hardware is reserved and ready so they don't run out of "virtual" room.

3. Microservices Architecture

The game backend is split into independent parts:

  • Matchmaking: One service handles finding opponents.
  • Battle Servers: Separate servers run the actual 3v3 match logic.
  • Supercell ID: A dedicated system (using ScyllaDB) handles social features and logins. Because these are separate, a bottleneck in the "Friends List" won't necessarily cause the actual game matches to lag.

4. Load Testing

Before a big week, engineers run "synthetic loads" where they simulate millions of "fake" players hitting the servers. This helps them find the "breaking point" of their code before real players do.

title: Prompted does supercell have their own server infra or do they use cloud hosting?

safeHtmlItem.html:
Supercell relies almost entirely on cloud hosting, specifically Amazon Web Services (AWS), to run its global game infrastructure. They have been a cloud-native company since their early days, choosing this model to allow their small, autonomous game teams (the "cells") to manage massive scale without needing a large internal IT operations department.

Key Infrastructure Details

  • Primary Cloud Provider: AWS is the backbone of their operations. They use Amazon EC2 for game server instances and Amazon Aurora (MySQL-compatible) for their primary databases to reduce downtime and handle millions of concurrent players.
  • Low-Latency Edge Services: To keep games like Brawl Stars and Clash Royale responsive, they utilize AWS Local Zones and Amazon CloudFront (CDN) to place compute and storage resources closer to players in major population centers.
  • Data Processing: Their analytics pipeline handles over 45 billion in-game events per day. They use Amazon Kinesis for real-time data streaming and Amazon S3 for long-term storage of petabytes of game data.
  • Supercell ID & Persistence: For services that require extreme speed and reliability, such as Supercell ID and friend-request routing, they have also integrated ScyllaDB Cloud, a fully managed NoSQL database known for single-digit millisecond latency.

Why not private servers?

Supercell’s philosophy is to keep game teams focused strictly on gameplay and features. By offloading "heavy lifting" like hardware maintenance and server scaling to AWS, a team of just three server developers can maintain thousands of instances for a game as large as Clash of Clans.

title: Prompted Is returning two phone cases in a row that I didn’t like to Amazon wrong? I mean the first one I never used, and the second one didn’t protect my phone at all, and was wildly scratched after about a week so returned that one pretty quick as well

safeHtmlItem.html:
Returning two items in a row isn't "wrong" in a moral sense, especially if the products didn't meet basic expectations or were poor quality. Amazon’s business model is built to absorb a high volume of returns, though there are a few practical factors to keep in mind regarding how they track this behavior.

The Reality of Returns

  • Product Misrepresentation: If a case is advertised as protective but fails to perform or arrives/quickly becomes damaged, it is considered "not as described" or "defective." Returning these is your right as a consumer.
  • The "Unused" Standard: Returning the first case unused is the ideal scenario for a retailer, as it can be easily processed or resold.
  • Account Health: Amazon uses algorithms to flag accounts with unusually high return-to-purchase ratios. While two returns won't trigger any red flags, a consistent pattern of returning a high percentage of what you buy can eventually lead to warnings or account restrictions.

Tips for the Next Purchase

To avoid the hassle of a third return, you might want to:

  • Check "Vine Customer Reviews": These are often more detailed regarding long-term durability.
  • Look for "Military Grade" Certifications: If protection is the priority, look for specific drop-test standards rather than just aesthetic descriptions.
  • Verify Material: Hard polycarbonate (PC) resists scratches better than soft silicone, which tends to attract lint and scuffs more easily.
